findings.quote: That a name is acceptable as long as the thing it borrows from comes in many versions.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: A is the only distractor with real verbatim footing. The passage does say "The occasional literal name survives only because the thing it borrows from comes in enough versions to swallow the error — brick, ash, sand." A student can cite that sentence and argue many-versioned borrowing is the stated criterion of acceptability. It is beatable on three counts. (i) The prompt asks about "the rule", and the passage names exactly one: "settled last, after the pigments are fixed, by two people with a spreadsheet and one rule. The rule is that a handle must not be checkable." (ii) A converts "survives only because" (a necessary condition on an exception) into "acceptable as long as" (a sufficient condition on the general case) — a logical inversion the text does not license. (iii) B subsumes A: many versions "swallow the error", i.e. make the name uncheckable, so the exception is an instance of the rule, while A cannot explain the main mechanism ("the winners drift toward places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed"). Not a second defensible answer; surfaced as the strongest distractor case in the batch. C is CLEAN (contradicted by "the names are not descriptions"), D is CLEAN (no trade colour standard appears in the passage). No distractor case is stronger than the key's support.

findings.quote: That a name is acceptable as long as the thing it borrows from comes in many versions.
findings.note: ARGUABLE (re-gated after the option edit; A's text is unchanged from the earlier run and the case against it still holds). A is the only distractor with verbatim footing: the passage's closing sentence reads "The occasional literal name survives only because the thing it borrows from comes in enough versions to swallow the error — brick, ash, sand." A student can cite that and argue many-versioned borrowing is the stated criterion of acceptability. It is beatable on three independent counts. (i) Prompt scope: the stem asks about "the rule that Bellamy & Roe applies", and the passage names exactly one — "settled last, after the pigments are fixed, by two people with a spreadsheet and one rule. The rule is that a handle must not be checkable." A describes the survival condition of an exception, not the rule. (ii) Logical inversion: A converts "survives only because" (a necessary condition on the exceptional case) into "acceptable as long as" (a sufficient condition on the general case); the text licenses neither move. (iii) Subsumption: enough versions to "swallow the error" is precisely what makes such a name uncheckable, so A's mechanism is an instance of B's rule, while A cannot account for the main pattern — "So the winners drift toward places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed." Not a second defensible answer, but the strongest distractor case in the unit. C is CLEAN: directly contradicted by "the names are not descriptions", and Tomato is the passage's own example of a recognizable name failing. D is CLEAN: no trade colour standard appears anywhere in the passage, and the text's logic runs the opposite way — names win by being undefendable-against, i.e. uncheckable. Key B ("no buyer is in a position to prove it inaccurate") is a faithful restatement of "must not be checkable", cross-checked by "a customer who grows tomatoes will say so at the counter". No distractor case is stronger than the key's support.
